description: Sou estudante de Educação Física, interessada em biomecânica, fisiologia do exercício e saúde espacial. Meu projeto propõe um sistema vestível de suporte biomecânico adaptativo integrado a exercícios ativos, visando investigar estratégias para preservar a função muscular e o controle da coluna em microgravidade. Busco formar uma equipe multidisciplinar com pessoas de engenharia, programação, robótica, design e pesquisa científica para desenvolver essa ideia.
summary:
OLEM is a wearable technology concept designed to monitor human movement and support adaptive exercise in microgravity-related research. The project proposes integrating flexible textile sensors, a load cell, and an ESP32 microcontroller into a wearable vest to collect biomechanical data, including trunk rotation, inclination, range of motion, and applied force.

We developed a conceptual system architecture and an initial software simulation using the Pallof Press exercise as a test case. The simulation analyzes movement data, identifies deviations, and generates feedback such as maintaining, reducing, or allowing exercise progression, while blocking progression when signal quality is compromised.

OLEM addresses the challenge of monitoring movement and exercise performance in environments where gravity changes the demands placed on the human body. It is important because it explores how wearable sensing and data-driven feedback could contribute to future exercise monitoring and biomechanical support technologies for human space exploration.
details:
Project Details — OLEM: Adaptive Biomechanical Support Wearable System

OLEM is a wearable technology concept designed to monitor trunk movement and exercise performance through an integrated system of flexible sensors, a load cell, and an ESP32 microcontroller.

How it works: Flexible sensors integrated into the vest are intended to detect textile deformation associated with trunk movements, while the load cell measures the force applied during resistance exercises. The ESP32 is planned to acquire and transmit these signals to a software system, where biomechanical variables can be processed, analyzed, and displayed through an interactive dashboard.

As an initial use case, we selected the Pallof Press, an anti-rotation exercise that allows us to investigate trunk stability under external resistance. Our Python simulation uses a hypothetical participant performing three repetitions, with trunk rotation values of 3°, 5°, and 12°. The algorithm identifies the increase in rotation and generates a simulated recommendation to reduce exercise difficulty. It can also block progression when signal quality is compromised.

Technology and tools: The proposed hardware includes flexible textile sensors, a load cell, and an ESP32 development board. Python is used for the initial data-processing and decision-rule simulation. TypeScript is proposed for the interactive monitoring dashboard, with Lovable serving as a platform for developing the web prototype.

Benefits and intended impact: OLEM explores a way to combine movement monitoring, applied-force measurement, and data-driven feedback in one wearable system. Its intended impact is to support research into exercise performance, biomechanical monitoring, and adaptive exercise technologies for future human space exploration. The concept may also inspire applications in terrestrial rehabilitation and movement research, subject to further investigation and validation.

Creativity and design considerations: The project's creative approach lies in integrating flexible sensing into wearable textiles and connecting biomechanical measurements to a software-based feedback system. Our team considered sensor placement, calibration requirements, signal reliability, movement variability, comfort, system feasibility, and safe responses to inconsistent data. We are following a progressive development strategy, beginning with software simulation before physical sensor integration and experimental validation.
